I need to determine the SMILES string of an unknown organic compound. To do this efficiently and minimize costs, I should start with the most informative and cost-effective analyses.

Let me start by getting the proton NMR spectra, as this is typically one of the most informative techniques for structure determination and can give me information about:
- Number and types of hydrogen environments
- Functional groups present
- Aromatic vs aliphatic protons

This will help me narrow down the structure before using more expensive techniques.

This suggests:
1. All 10 protons are in the aromatic region (7.51 ppm)
2. They appear to be equivalent or very similar in chemical environment
3. The molecule likely has a high degree of symmetry

A compound with 10 aromatic protons could be:
- Naphthalene (C10H8) - but this has only 8 protons
- Azulene (C10H8) - also 8 protons
- A substituted benzene with additional aromatic groups
- Two benzene rings connected somehow

Let me get the carbon NMR to understand the carbon framework better.

The carbon NMR shows:
- 13 carbon signals (with some appearing multiple times due to symmetry)
- One signal at 196.40 ppm - this is characteristic of a carbonyl carbon (C=O), likely a ketone
- Multiple signals in the aromatic region (128-137 ppm)
- The pattern suggests two equivalent phenyl groups

- 196.40 (1 carbon) - carbonyl
- 137.56 (appears twice) - aromatic
- 131.90 (appears twice) - aromatic  
- 130.00 (appears 4 times) - aromatic
- 128.40 (appears 4 times) - aromatic

This pattern is consistent with benzophenone (diphenyl ketone): (C6H5)2CO
- Molecular formula: C13H10O
- It has a carbonyl group connecting two phenyl rings
- The two phenyl rings are equivalent, explaining the symmetry
- 10 aromatic protons (5 on each ring)
- The carbonyl carbon would appear around 196 ppm

</thought>

- Peaks around 1580-1592 cm⁻¹ - aromatic C=C stretches

This strongly supports benzophenone structure. The carbonyl at 1697 cm⁻¹ is consistent with a diaryl ketone.
